newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian fund managers get style benchmarks.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian fund managers get style benchmarks.

text.p: Investors now have a tool to judge the performance of Australian funds according to their investment style after the recent introduction of a set of benchmarks by investment consultant Frank Russell Australia in conjunction with the Australian Stock Exchange (ASX).

Style analysis was developed in the 1970s as a way of explaining the different approaches fund managers take to evaluating securities. Despite a high degree of sophistication in its financial markets, Australia has lagged well behind North America and Europe in adopting style benchmarks.
"Australian funds have traditionally compared returns to the All Ordinaries index, regardless of the manager's investment style," ASX index officer, Andrew Black told Reuters.
"This means that different styles have risen and fallen in favour based on the difference between the performance of the styles and the market," he said.

Russell's model of stock returns splits the investment decision into two key factors - firstly, the company's size and secondly, whether its stock is attractive due to its earnings growth, or because of its relative value.

Introduced in June this year, the Russell/ASX indexes are based on three existing ASX indexes, the All Ordinaries, the ASX 100 and the Small Ordinaries. The stocks within these indexes have been split into growth and value components to create six new indexes which separately track their performance.

"There has been a degree of cynicism about whether the indexes will be as applicable to the Australian markets as they have been in other markets," said Scott Donald, a client manager at Frank Russell Australia.

Donald said the nature of the Australian market offered more opportunity for top-down approaches to work rather than approaches to valuing stocks. "You do tend to see more a market-orientated type manager who actually looks at the whole market, based on a view as to which way the economy is going."
Donald said that top-down type fund managers often tended to rotate between growth and value styles.

"What our research has shown to date is that there are a number of (fund managers) that follow a value style, a smaller number who follow a growth style and quite a number do seem to be rotating consciously or unconsciously across the styles."

Rather than using price/earnings multiples, the Russell/ASX indexes calculate price to net tangible asset (NTA) multiples as a means of separating value from growth stocks because it has found this to be a reliable and easily available measure.

Stocks are ranked from low to high and then separated into quartiles. First quartile stocks with a low price to NTA, below 1.6, are classed as all value style. Those ranked in the fourth quartile, above 3.3 are classed as all growth style.
The 50 percent in between can have varying degrees of value and growth depending on where they fit.
"In the U.S. the experience has been growth stocks can lag value stocks for extended periods of time, then their catch up is remarkably swift," Donald said.

Donald said empirical evidence suggested the catch-up period for growth stocks usually occurred when there was a weaker economic outlook and consequently a scarcity of stocks offering growth potential.
